Read the following case based passage and answer the questions given after passage.
Hans Christian Oersted (1777-1851) observed that a compass needle suffers a deflection when placed near a metal wire carrying an electric current. This discovery gave the first evidence of a connection between electric and magnetic phenomena. Andre Ampere (1775-1836) grasped the significance of Oersted's discovery. He carried out a large series of experiments to explore the relationship between current electricity and magnetism. On the basis of experiments, he hypothesised that all magnetic phenomena are due to circulated electric currents. Later on many devices such as electromagnets, electric motors, microphones, electric generators, etc. were developed on the basis of magnetic phenomena.
(i) A magnetic needle is a/an
(a) isolated north pole pivoted at its centre of mass.
(b) isolated south pole pivoted at its centre of mass.
(c) ordinary needle made of soft iron and pivoted at its centre of mass.
(d) small bar magnet pivoted at its centre of mass.
(ii) A freely suspended magnet always rests in geographically north and south direction because:
(a) the Earth has two poles.
(b) the Earth behaves as a huge magnet.
(c) the magnetic north pole of the Earth's magnet is located very close to its south pole.
(d) the magnetic south pole of the Earth's magnet is located very close to its south pole.
items.answer:
(i) (d) small bar magnet pivoted at its centre of mass. A magnetic needle is simply a tiny bar magnet, free to turn about a pivot at its centre of mass; magnetic poles never exist in isolation.
(ii) (b) the Earth behaves as a huge magnet. The Earth's own magnetic field acts on the suspended magnet and turns it until it lies along the field, that is, roughly along the geographic north-south direction.
items.ocr: The printed sub-part (iii) ('When a current flows through a straight conductor, a magnetic field is produced around it. Consider the following statements about this field: I. The direction of the magnetic field of a current carrying straight conductor is determined by right-hand thumb rule.') is cut off by a page split at '## Page 37' - statements II/III, its options and the whole printed answer key for question 178 never extracted, so (iii) is dropped rather than published half-formed. No 'Ans' block survives for this case at all; the answers given for (i) and (ii) are derived from the passage and standard physics, and are flagged here as reconstructed. Page furniture ('## Page 37') stripped; the section heading is printed as 'CASE BASED QUEATIONS' (sic) and kept verbatim.

items.stem:
Read the following case based passage and answer the questions given after passage.
Usually, electric appliances with high power rating such as heaters, irons, etc., have a terminal for connecting the earth wire, in addition to terminals for the live and neutral wires. The earth wire is connected to the metallic body of the appliance. This is done to avoid shocks in case of a fault. Suppose, due to some reason, the insulation of the live wire inside an electric iron gets burnt at a place. If the metallic body of the iron is in contact with the defective wire, it will be at a potential of 220 V when the iron is in use. If a person accidentally touches the metallic body of the iron, he/she will get an electric shock. However, with the earth wire properly connected to the metallic body, the current will quickly go to the earth and the potential of the metallic body will not rise. Thus, earthing of electric appliances protects us from electric shock.
(Figure: failed insulation brings the live wire into contact with the metal case.)
(i) What is the application of earth wire?
(ii) What are different types of wires used in an electric circuit?
(iii) Earth is good conductor or bad conductor of electricity?
items.answer:
(i) The earth wire is connected to the metallic body of the appliance. This is done to avoid shocks in case of a fault: if the live wire touches the metal body, the fault current runs harmlessly to the earth and the body never rises to 220 V.
(ii) Live, neutral and earth wire.
(iii) Good. The earth is a good conductor of electricity, which is why it can carry the leakage current away.
items.ocr: The page-37 illustration of a faulty iron is attached, but figure_required is left false because all three sub-parts are answerable from the passage text alone. The dangling caption line 'Failed insulation brings wire into contact with metal case', which MinerU printed as running text just before the image, has been turned into a parenthetical figure caption. A missing question mark added to sub-part (iii).

Read the following case based passage and answer the questions given after passage. The mobile phone is an excellent communication device. Mobile phones uses electromagnetic radiation in the microwave range. Part of the radio wave emitted by the mobile phone handset will be absorbed by the head. Head is in the 'near field' of radiation, so that most of the heating effect occurs in the head. Temperature in the internal ear, brain increases by 1 degree or more. This adversely affect the functioning of these organs since these have fluid filled cavities. But prolonged heating effect can alter brain functions and hearing ability also. Other harmful effects such as Premature Cataract, Confusion and loss of memory may also be possible. Following figure shows that how mobile phone radiation penetrates the brain.

Absorption rate: 4.49 W/kg Source: Electronic Engineer'sAbsorption 3.21 W/kg Institute ofrate: Absorption rate 2.93 W/kg Electrical and journal on
(i) What precautions should be taken while using mobile phones? (ii) Which radiations are used in mobile phones? (iii) How does prolonged heating effect due to mobile radiations can effect adversely? (iv) In which part of our body, most of the heating effect occurs due to use of mobiles?
items.answer:
(i) Try to consider mobile phone as a communication device and not an entertainment device. Even if you are not talking, the cell phone is emitting strong signals to keep a link with the base station, so keep calls short and keep the handset away from the head.
(ii) Electromagnetic radiations of microwave range are used in mobile phones.
(iii) Heating effect can alter brain functions and hearing ability also. Other harmful effects such as premature cataract, confusion and loss of memory may also be possible.

items.stem:
Read the following case based passage and answer the questions given after passage.
Domestic electric circuits has main board which contains the meter (energy-meter) and the main switch. From the street electric pole a thick rubber insulated cord reaches the main board. It contains two thick copper or aluminium wires, one covered with red and the other covered with black (or brown) plastic covering. They form the live line wire (L) and neutral line wire (N) respectively. Live line has a potential of 220 V whereas the neutral wire has zero potential (with respect to the earth). They enter the main board and are connected to the meter. Inside the house, connections to all the devices are made in parallel, each having independent switch and fuse (if necessary). Thus, whenever some fault occurs in circuit of one particular device in one room, devices in other rooms do not suffer. The figure shows a 240 V AC mains circuit to which a number of appliances (a 1.2 kW fan circuit, a 200 W refrigerator and two 60 W lamps) are connected and switched on.
(i) Calculate the power supplied to the circuit.
(ii) Find out the value of electric current in the refrigerators.
(iii) Calculate energy used by the fan in 2 hours.
(iv) Calculate resistance of the filament of one lamp.
items.answer:
(i) Power supplied to the circuit
= 1.2 × 1000 W + 200 W + 60 W + 60 W
= 1200 W + 200 W + 60 W + 60 W
= 1520 W = 1.52 kW
(ii) Current in the refrigerator = Power / Voltage = 200 W / 240 V = 0.83 A
(iii) Energy used by the fan in 2 hours = Power × Time
= 1.2 kW × 2 h
= 1.2 × 1000 J/s × 2 × 60 × 60 s
= 1200 × 2 × 3600 J
= 8 640 000 J = 8.64 × 10⁶ J
(iv) Current in one lamp, I = P/V = 60/240 = 0.25 A
Resistance, R = V/I = 240/0.25 = 960 Ω
items.ocr: figure_required is true: the appliance ratings (1.2 kW fan, 200 W refrigerator, two 60 W lamps) and the 240 V supply are printed only inside the circuit diagram, so none of the four parts can be worked without it; the ratings are also summarised in the stem for readability. LaTeX arrays rewritten to Unicode: $1.2 \times 1000 \mathrm{W}$ -> 1.2 × 1000 W, $\frac{\mathrm{Power}}{\mathrm{Voltage}}$ -> Power / Voltage, $\Omega$ -> Ω, $8.64 \times 10^{7}$ -> see next note. CONFLICT: the printed key for (iii) ends '= 86400000 J = 8.64 × 10^7 J', but its own preceding line reads 1200 × 2 × 3600 J, which is 8 640 000 J. The worked solution wins, so the answer is given as 8.64 × 10⁶ J (the printed final value carries one extra zero). 'They from the live line wire' corrected to 'They form the live line wire'. Page furniture ('## Page 42') stripped.

items.stem:
Read the following case based passage and answer the questions given after passage.
Though the concepts of both electricity and magnet were discovered earlier, any type of relation between the two was still unknown till the beginning of 19th century. It was in 1819 that Hans Christian Oersted discovered this relation somewhat accidentally. He placed a current carrying wire over a compass; the needle of the compass turned 90° to the axis of the wire. When the direction of the current was reversed the position of the needle also reversed. This gave Oersted the idea that the electric current is causing the magnetic effect with specific directional properties. This idea gave birth to the concept of 'Electromagnetism'.
(i) When the compass is placed over the wire carrying current, the needle of the compass faces in which direction?
(a) Parallel to the current flow.
(b) Perpendicular to the current flow.
(c) Diagonal to the current flow.
(d) Is not directly related to the direction of current flow.
(ii) When the direction of the current flow is reversed, how does it affect the direction of the magnetic field produced?
(a) It changes 180°
(b) It changes 90°
(c) Does not change
(d) Cannot be determined due to Bohr's indeterminacy
items.answer:
(i) (b) Perpendicular to the current flow. The magnetic field of a straight current-carrying wire is made of circles in the plane at right angles to the wire, so a compass placed over the wire sets itself perpendicular to it.
(ii) (a) It changes 180°. Reversing the current reverses the sense of the circular field (right-hand thumb rule), so the field at every point points the opposite way and the needle turns through 180°.
items.ocr: This case is the last block of the extraction and is split by MinerU's page ordering: the passage and sub-parts (i) and (ii) (options a-c only) sit at the end of page 42, while option (d) of (ii), 'Cannot be determined due to Bohr's indeterminacy', and the printed key 'Ans (i) (b) Perpendicular to the current flow. (ii) (a) It changes 180c' were carried to the top of page 39 (char ~122.8k), just before question 186. The two halves have been rejoined. '90^{\circ}' / '180c' / '90c' rewritten to 90° and 180°. Typos repaired: 'He placed a current carrying over a compass' -> 'He placed a current carrying wire over a compass'; 'the positioned of the needle' -> 'the position of the needle'; a missing question mark added to (ii).

items.stem:
Read the following case based passage and answer the questions given after passage.
Magnetic field is a quantity that has both direction and magnitude. The direction of the magnetic field is taken to be the direction in which a north pole of the compass needle moves inside it. Therefore, it is taken by convention that the field lines emerge from north pole and merge at the south pole. Inside the magnet, the direction of field lines is from its south pole to its north pole. Thus the magnetic field lines are closed curves. The relative strength of the magnetic field is shown by the degree of closeness of the field lines. The field is stronger, that is, the force acting on the pole of another magnet placed there is greater, where the field lines are crowded. No two field-lines are found to cross each other. If they did, it would mean that at the point of intersection, the compass needle would point towards two directions, which is not possible.
(i) The direction of magnetic field lines inside a magnet is from:
(a) One end to another end
(b) One pole to another pole
(c) South pole to north pole
(d) North pole to south pole
(ii) The strength of a magnet is more at the poles than at the middle because:
(a) The magnetic field lines intersect at the poles but not at the middle of the magnet.
(b) There is no magnetic field line at the middle of the magnet.
(c) The magnetic field lines are more crowded at the middle than at the poles.
(d) The magnetic field lines are more crowded at the poles than at the middle.
(iii) Which of the following statement is correct about the magnetic lines of force?
(a) The magnetic field lines are closed curves
(b) No two field lines intersect to each other
(c) The field lines emerge from south pole and merge at the north pole
(d) Both (a) and (b)
(iv) Which of the following statement is correct about the magnetic field?
(a) Magnetic field is a quantity that has both direction and magnitude.
(b) Magnetic field is a quantity that has only direction but no magnitude.
(c) Magnetic field is a quantity that has only magnitude but no direction.
(d) All of the above.
items.answer:
(i) (c) South pole to north pole.
(ii) (d) The magnetic field lines are more crowded at the poles than at the middle.
(iii) (d) Both (a) and (b) - magnetic field lines are closed curves and no two of them ever intersect; option (c) is wrong because the lines emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole outside the magnet.
(iv) (a) Magnetic field is a quantity that has both direction and magnitude, as stated in the opening line of the passage.
items.ocr: MinerU shuffled this case badly. The printed sub-parts arrived in the order (i), (ii), (v), (iii), with a fifth sub-part '(iv) Which of the following figure represents the correct representation of magnetic field lines around a bar magnet ?' dropped into the middle of the passage; its four answer figures never extracted, so that unanswerable part is omitted and the remaining four are renumbered in sequence - the item's (iv) is the printed (v). Lost option labels restored in the printed (v): only '(a)' and '(d)' survived, so 'Magnetic field is a quantity that has only direction but no magnitude.' was relabelled (b) and 'Magnetic field is a quantity that has only magnitude but no direction.' relabelled (c). A stray OCR character 'b' after option (d) of sub-part (i) was dropped, and 'field fines' corrected to 'field lines'. The printed key stops after two parts ('Ans (i) (c) South pole to north pole (ii) (d) ...') where the advertisement line 'Click Here to Buy book on Amazon' and a page break cut it off; the answers to the last two parts are derived from the passage and flagged here as reconstructed. Page furniture ('## Page 40', 'Click Here to Buy book on Amazon') stripped.

items.stem:
Read the following case based passage and answer the questions given after passage.
During winters, you would like to sit near a heater or fire place. If you sit nearby heater, you feel more warmth but if you are far away from it, you feel warmth is less. Similarly, a bar magnet has a region or space surrounding it where other substances can experience a force of attraction or repulsion but the magnitude of force depends upon the distance between them as well as on the strength of magnet. The more the distance, the smaller the force. So, the region or space around a magnet where magnetic force can be experienced by other magnetic substance is called magnetic field.
(i) SI unit of magnetic field is
(a) henry
(b) weber
(c) newton
(d) tesla
(ii) A bar magnet has strongest magnetism
(a) at one quarter distance from the poles of the magnet
(b) near the poles of the magnet
(c) at the centre of the magnet
(d) inside of the magnet
(iii) Magnetic field lines can be used to determine
(a) only the relative strength of the magnetic field
(b) only the direction of magnetic field
(c) both the direction and relative strength of the magnetic field
(d) the shape of the magnetic field
(iv) The magnetism of bar magnet at the centre of magnet is:
(a) same as the pole
(b) zero
(c) maximum
(d) minimum
(v) Magnetic field is produced by the flow of current in a straight wire. The phenomenon was discovered by
(a) Faraday
(b) Fleming
(c) Oersted
(d) Maxwell
items.answer:
(i) (d) tesla
(ii) (b) near the poles of the magnet
(iii) (c) both the direction and relative strength of the magnetic field
(iv) (d) minimum
(v) (c) Oersted
items.ocr: The page-41 bar-magnet field figure is attached, but figure_required is left false because all five sub-parts are answerable from the passage text alone. Lost option labels restored: sub-part (i) printed as 'SI unit of magnetic field is henry (b) weber newton (d) tesla', so 'henry' was relabelled (a) and 'newton' relabelled (c); sub-part (iv) printed as '... is: same as the pole (b) zero (c) maximum (d) minimum', so 'same as the pole' was relabelled (a). The printed key is kept as printed for (iv) ('(d) minimum'), even though (b) 'zero' would be the stricter reading of the field at the centre of a bar magnet - the key and the four options are internally consistent as printed, so no conflict was recorded against the solution.
